title: The Word is the Guru
hook: the yogis ask who Nanak's guru is, and he answers: the Word is the Guru, attention is the disciple

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked where the mind lives, and Nanak said the Word steadies it. Your line was the word steadies. Did a line bring you home? Today they ask whose Word it is. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

Who did you study with? Ask a classical musician and you'll often hear a name, and behind that name another, a line of teachers going back through the years. In that world your teacher is part of who you are. The yogis Nanak met also spoke of teachers and their disciples. So sooner or later, in the Sidh Gosht, they ask the obvious question. What is the root of all this? And who is your guru? Whose disciple are you? Today: the Word is the Guru.
screen: `WHO DID YOU STUDY WITH?` → `A LINE OF TEACHERS.` → `WHO IS YOUR GURU, NANAK?`

segments.voice: Here's the answer, and this time a few of the original words are worth hearing: sabad guroo, surat dhun chelaa. Sabad is the Word, the shabad. Guroo, the Guru. Surat is attention, awareness. Dhun is the tune, the strain of the music. Chelaa is the disciple. So, in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. He goes on: speaking the unspoken, he stays unattached, and through all the ages, the Lord of the world is his Guru. Look at what he doesn't say. He gives no human name, no line of teachers to check. The yogis asked for a person, and he gives them a relationship. On one side, the Word. On the other, your own attention, tuned to it, the way a string is tuned to a note. A guru, in this answer, isn't someone you trace back. It's something you listen to now. And the disciple isn't a body sitting at someone's feet. It's the part of you that pays attention. That has a strong practical side. It means anyone who listens can be a disciple, today, wherever they are. Teaching isn't something you get by being in the right lineage; it reaches whoever tunes in. It also explains something about Sikh life. Sikhs today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of hymns, as the Guru. When a visitor first sees that, it can seem surprising. In this stanza, Guru Nanak had already answered the yogis that way: the Word is the Guru. That's today's line. The word is guru.
screen: `SABAD GUROO, SURAT DHUN CHELAA.` · `NO HUMAN NAME, NO LINEAGE.` · `ATTENTION IS THE DISCIPLE.` · `THE GRANTH, HONORED AS GURU.` · then, large: `THE WORD IS GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tune your attention for two minutes. If you can, play a shabad, any one you love, quietly. If not, let one line of Gurbani you know sit in the silence, or simply Waheguru. Now be the disciple in the stanza: not a body at someone's feet, just attention. Let it rest on the sound, the way a string settles on a note. When it drifts, that's the string going slack; bring it gently back into tune. You aren't trying to understand every word. You're only listening, which in this answer is what a disciple does. If you pray, the listening itself can be the prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Word is the Guru. Sabad guroo, surat dhun chelaa: Nanak's answer to the yogis, the Word as Guru and tuned attention as the disciple. Today's word.
screen: `THE WORD IS THE GURU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the word is guru. Once today, when you hear something true, in a hymn, a book or a friend's voice, stop and give it your full attention, the way a student would. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, bowing before it in the gurdwara, and often cite 'sabad guroo surat dhun chelaa' when explaining why the Word, not a human lineage, is the Guru.

fork.setup: you're a yogi, and your own teacher has a name and a lineage. you ask Nanak: who is your guru, whose disciple are you? what does he say?
options: he names his teacher and his teacher's teacher.
the Word is the Guru, and tuned attention is the disciple.
he has no need of any guru.
fork.reveal: sabad guroo, surat dhun chelaa: no human name, but a Guru all the same, and a disciple anyone can be.

original.note: the Word is the Guru; attention tuned to it is the disciple.

trapdoor: what you thought: a guru is a person with a lineage of teachers.
what it means: Nanak tells the yogis the Word is the Guru, and tuned attention is the disciple.
what a scholar hears: this stanza is a key text for Sikh understanding of the shabad as Guru, later honored in the Guru Granth Sahib.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Mahala 1, Sidh Gosht, pauris 43–44, Ang 942–943 (who is your guru; sabad guroo surat dhun chelaa)

notes: Pauris 43–44 paraphrased: the yogis ask the root, the teaching of the age, and who is your guru, whose disciple are you; Nanak: from the air the beginning, the age of the True Guru's teaching, sabad guroo surat dhun chelaa, speaking the unspoken I remain detached, through the ages the Lord of the world is my guru. The 'air' line is not explained in the script. Please confirm.
Gloss of the five words (sabad, guroo, surat, dhun, chelaa) given as standard meanings, not etymologies. Please confirm.
The opening of pauri 44 ('from the air came the beginning') was left out to keep the day to one idea.
Trapdoor floor 3 calls the stanza 'a key text' for the shabad as Guru; please confirm this description is fair or soften it.
Hook's description of classical musicians and yogic lineages is general; flagged for checking.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced claim that for yogis 'a guru had a guru, and the line was the proof that the teaching was real', replaced with a plain remark that the yogis spoke of teachers and disciples (the poem's own question 'whose disciple are you' supports this); varied the practice's closing prayer line.
